source_scope: 34 non-archived TheAlgorithms algorithm repositories. Portable-language source paths can supply benchmark implementations; AArch64 Assembly paths are included only as discovery references.
matching_method: Normalize each source filename stem (including camelCase to snake_case); Project Euler solN files include their problem number. Identical normalized stems are candidate matches only and have not been checked for equivalent behavior.
excluded_paths: Tests, examples, benchmarks, documentation, scripts, build output, and vendor directories are omitted.

source_repositories.usage: discovery reference only; architecture-specific assembly is not a portable benchmark implementation

candidates.review_notes: The pinned Dart source uses the direct recursive include-or-exclude recurrence without memoization. It is kept distinct from the bottom-up tabulation benchmark so their runtime and call-stack behavior can be compared. The shared contract bounds the item count to 16 to keep the exponential recurrence practical and defines malformed inputs explicitly.

The pinned C++ source fills a bottom-up 0/1 knapsack table with the same item/capacity recurrence as the canonical tabulation candidate. This filename is retained as an alias to share one workload and contract.

The pinned C LeetCode source solves the Two Sum problem with nested scans under the source problem's single-solution assumption. It overwrites the result for each matching pair, so multiple matches select the last pair in scan order, and a no-solution input returns a zero-filled pair. The shared benchmark defines an explicit no-pair sentinel and a deterministic earliest-pair rule; this numeric filename is reviewed as an alias of that standardized Two Sum contract.

The pinned C LeetCode source performs recursive full-string matching with '.' for one character and '*' for zero or more repetitions of its preceding atom. It has the same matching semantics as the Python recursive_match implementation and aliases that contract.

The pinned C LeetCode source computes the maximum subarray sum over adjacent price differences with Kadane's algorithm. This is equivalent to the single-buy/single-sell maximum-profit contract and aliases the shared stock benchmark.
The pinned C LeetCode source XORs all signed 32-bit values, which returns the single value when every other value occurs twice. It aliases the shared single_number XOR contract.
The pinned C LeetCode source checks positivity and applies the standard n & (n - 1) power-of-two predicate, matching the existing signed 64-bit benchmark semantics on the source's integer domain.

The pinned C LeetCode source reverses half the digits and compares the halves. It matches the shared nonnegative signed-32-bit palindrome-number contract; negative inputs are outside that contract because the Dart source throws on them.

Inspected the pinned C-Sharp, Dart, F-Sharp, both Go, JavaScript, Julia, Lua, Mojo, Nim, Python, Ruby, Rust, Scala, and Solidity sources. They provide absolute magnitude operations for integer or numeric inputs; Go also includes a bitwise integer version, and several files provide min/max helpers. The shared benchmark selects signed 64-bit integers, returns -1 when INT64_MIN has no representable positive result, and exposes the distinct C-ABI symbol abs_i64.

The pinned Java implementation selects by absolute magnitude and resolves equal magnitudes in favor of the greater signed value. The PHP function performs ordinary numeric maximum and is recorded as a semantic mismatch.

The pinned Java implementation selects by absolute magnitude and resolves equal magnitudes in favor of the smaller signed value. The PHP function performs ordinary numeric minimum and is recorded as a semantic mismatch.

The pinned Java and TypeScript sources return the same integer absolute-value mapping as the canonical abs candidate. This filename is retained as an alias and shares the signed 64-bit overflow contract.

The pinned Java method compares the sum of all divisors with twice the input, which is equivalent to checking whether the positive proper-divisor sum exceeds the number. The Python abundant_numbers implementation checks the same predicate by divisor pairs. The shared contract bounds positive inputs to 1,000,000,000 and defines an out-of-range sentinel.
The pinned Python plural-name file implements the same abundant-number predicate as the canonical Java candidate and shares its benchmark contract.

The C++ example returns zero for zero and one, Nim accepts a positive input type, and Rust panics on zero. The local contract explicitly defines zero, negative inputs, result width, and overflow behavior while preserving the divisor scan.
The pinned Rust source rotates both uppercase and lowercase ASCII letters by thirteen and copies other characters unchanged, matching the shared case-preserving ASCII ROT13 contract.

The pinned Java utility converts a validated base-2-through-36 digit string through decimal into another radix. The local array contract preserves its radix and uppercase-digit semantics and adds checked signed 64-bit accumulation for portable cross-language behavior.
The Java source converts radix digits to an integer. The shared contract encodes digits as 0-35 in most-significant-first order and rejects invalid digits or values outside signed 64-bit range.

The pinned JavaScript source converts between arbitrary character alphabets by folding source digits to an integer and re-encoding in the target alphabet. Under the shared standard digit alphabet and signed 64-bit contract, it is the same base-conversion algorithm as any_base_to_any_base.

The eight pinned files collect overlapping formulas for plane areas and solid surface areas. The shared benchmark covers 22 shape formulas under a bounded, deterministic fixed-point contract. Generic polygon shoelace area is tracked separately as area_of_polygon; callback-based trapezoidal integration is excluded from this shape-formula set.

The C reference uses integer exponentiation and an `int` input; C++ uses floating-point `std::pow` and handles negative values; Rust uses unsigned 32-bit digits and powers. The local contract uses the full signed 64-bit input range, exact integer arithmetic, and an integer predicate result.

The pinned Python and Rust sources provide Base16 encoding and strict uppercase decoding. The shared mode-based array contract covers both directions, rejects lowercase and malformed encodings, and uses the same byte output representation in all target languages.

The pinned Python and Rust sources provide Base32 encoding and decoding with the RFC 4648 alphabet. The shared contract accepts canonical padded or valid unpadded uppercase byte input, checks canonical trailing bits, and records portable ports in all nine target languages.

The pinned Go, Java, and Rust sources implement Base64 byte encoding and decoding. The benchmark normalizes them to one RFC 4648 byte-array contract, accepts canonical padded or valid unpadded input, and includes portable implementations in all nine target languages.

The pinned Python source repeatedly divides by -2 and adjusts negative remainders to emit 0/1 digits. The local contract returns canonical digit bytes for every signed 64-bit input, avoiding the upstream representation as a decimal integer.

The pinned PHP source repeatedly collects remainders and reverses them. Within the normalized domain of nonnegative values and bases 2 through 10, it is the same positional conversion as decimal_to_any_base; bases above 10 are excluded because the source does not encode alphabetic digits.

The inspected C and C++ sources use signed int distances and sentinel-based reachability; the C++ source also indexes a vector after reserving capacity without resizing it. The Rust source uses a generic ordered-map graph and predecessor results. The local benchmark uses an explicit directed edge-list ABI with signed 64-bit weights, separate reachability flags, checked addition, and a documented error status for reachable negative cycles.

The pinned Python source tracks the lowest price and best later sale for one transaction. The pinned C LeetCode and Java stock-profit sources implement equivalent semantics; the shared contract defines empty input, price bounds, and malformed-input behavior.

The C and C++ examples binary-search the sorted prefix before shifting larger items; their recursive search boundaries differ, and the C midpoint expression does not consistently account for the lower bound. Rust uses a lower-bound helper and rotates a slice. The local stable contract uses an upper-bound search and signed 64-bit values.

The inspected implementations all use binary search on sorted input but vary in API, sort direction, and duplicate-hit conventions. The local benchmark standardizes ascending signed 64-bit values and any matching index, or -1 when absent; workload values are unique.

The 12 pinned sources share unbalanced binary-search-tree ordering and operations such as insert, search, delete, extrema, or traversal, but differ on duplicates and API details. The benchmark standardizes unique-key set semantics, predecessor-based deletion, and a bounded index pool.

Inspected the pinned C, Dart, Java, JavaScript, PHP, Python, Ruby, Rust, and Swift sources. They convert binary digit sequences to their decimal value, taking bits from strings or decimal-encoded digits; the C and Rust sources validate the input, while Dart and Python also support a leading negative sign. The shared benchmark selects unsigned bits, represented as a most-significant-first array of at most 63 elements so results fit signed 64-bit.

Inspected the pinned C, Dart, Java, and Python sources. They convert decimal-encoded binary digits or binary strings to hexadecimal text, with differing validation, sign, case, and prefix behavior. The cataloged Rust path does not resolve at its pinned revision, so it was not used to infer the shared contract. The benchmark accepts a most-significant-first bit array of length 1 through 63, validates bits 0 and 1, and writes prefix-free lowercase hexadecimal output.

Inspected the pinned C, Dart, Java, and Python sources. They convert decimal-encoded binary digits or binary strings to octal text, with differing validation and signed-input behavior. The cataloged Rust path does not resolve at its pinned revision, so it was not used to infer the shared contract. The benchmark accepts a most-significant-first bit array of length 1 through 63, validates bits 0 and 1, and writes prefix-free octal output.

The pinned Rust source groups all copies of each current minimum value at the front, but loops through every integer from the minimum to maximum. The shared contract keeps the grouping strategy and locates the next present value in the remaining suffix, avoiding work proportional to empty numeric gaps and supporting signed 64-bit boundaries. Inputs are capped at 1024 values.

The pinned sources compute the binomial coefficient C(n,k), with Java and Python using Pascal-triangle/recursive formulations and Rust using an arbitrary-precision multiplicative recurrence. The Python implementation returns 1 for (n=0,k>0) because it handles zero before k>n; the local contract uses the standard definition and returns 0 when k>n. Rust assumes k<=n and subtracts unsigned values, so the local implementation validates this case. The shared binary-scalar contract supports n<=66, exact results in signed 64-bit range, and returns -1 for larger n.

The pinned C++ implementation supports directed or bidirectional edges and returns all visited vertices; the Rust implementation uses directed edges and returns history only until a requested target. The shared contract normalizes both APIs to a complete directed traversal in deterministic ascending-neighbor order.

The checked C and C++ implementations compare adjacent values, swap out-of-order pairs, and stop early after a pass without swaps. The local contract sorts signed 64-bit values in ascending order in place and is stable.

The pinned Java and Python sources perform one adjacent-swap pass and recurse on the shortened prefix only if a swap occurred. The Java version mutates in place; Python slices the prefix and returns a new list. The shared contract uses in-place sorting of signed 64-bit values and caps length at 256. The early-exit behavior distinguishes it from recursive_bubble_sort, which recurses after every pass.
The pinned C-Sharp class implements adjacent-swap bubble sort with an early exit after a pass makes no swaps. It shares the canonical bubble_sort ordering contract and workload.
The pinned C and Go catalan sources compute the standard indexed Catalan sequence; both filenames alias the exact scalar catalan_number contract.

Pinned C, C++, C-Sharp, Go, Java, JavaScript, Julia, Nim, Python, R, and Rust sources cover the standard Catalan sequence, using direct formulas, dynamic programming, or sequence generation. The exact scalar benchmark returns C(n) for indices 0 through 35. The second Rust source under src/math returns values modulo 1,000,000,007 and is a distinct output variant outside this contract.

The pinned C++, JavaScript, Nim, Python, R, and Rust dynamic-programming sources compute the standard Catalan sequence. The Rust src/math file instead applies a modulus and is documented as a distinct variant outside the exact scalar contract.
The pinned C-Sharp CatalanSequence yields the standard exact Catalan sequence; its indexed values share the catalan_number contract.
The pinned Go CatalanNumber function computes an indexed value of the standard Catalan sequence; the filename aliases catalan_number.

Reviewed the eight pinned sources in C-Sharp, Java, Julia, Mojo, Python, Ruby, Rust, and Zig. They aim to compute mathematical ceiling but vary in numeric bounds; Java preserves nonfinite or out-of-int-range values, Rust narrows through i32, and the current Zig implementation returns positive fractional inputs unchanged. The shared benchmark uses exact rational inputs with a positive denominator and checks mathematical ceiling using integer arithmetic.
The pinned C++ copies and PHP source named check_prime all implement scalar primality by trial division. They share prime_check’s explicit signed 32-bit positive input range and result contract.

The pinned Dart, Java, JavaScript, Python, Ruby, and TypeScript sources implement bounded FIFO queues using circular buffers. Their capacities and empty/full signaling differ, while the queue operation contract is the same. The canonical queue benchmark already includes capacity overflow, empty operations, and a full wraparound trace, so this filename is recorded as an alias rather than a duplicate benchmark.

The two pinned C++ copies scan the active range for its minimum and maximum, then place both at opposite ends before shrinking the range. Their swap logic can misplace the maximum when it starts at the low endpoint: moving the minimum changes the maximum index, but the source reuses the old index. The shared contract follows the iterative two-ended selection strategy and updates that index after the first swap. It sorts signed 64-bit values in place up to length 1024.
The pinned C-Sharp class makes forward and backward adjacent-swap passes while shrinking both active bounds, matching the cocktail_sort contract.

Inspected the pinned files across all 13 source repositories, including both Java files. The C++, Dart, Java dynamic-programming, Julia, R, Ruby, Rust, TypeScript, and Zig sources include minimum-coin change; JavaScript and Ruby also expose combination counting, Scala counts combinations, and the Lua and Java greedy files return a currency-dependent coin list. The local contract selects minimum count with unlimited positive denominations, defines zero amount as 0 and unreachable or invalid input as -1, and caps amount and denomination count for a fixed-array portable ABI.

The two pinned C++ top-down sources recursively solve the same unlimited-denomination minimum-coin problem as coin_change. Their memo table is passed by value and their unreachable-case sentinel is not robust, so the shared contract supplies explicit unreachable and invalid-input results.

The checked C and C++ sources shrink the comparison gap by about 1.3 and swap out-of-order pairs. The local contract uses a portable rational 10/13 shrink, enforces a minimum gap of one, and completes a no-swap adjacent pass before returning.
The pinned C-Sharp class shrinks the comparison gap by its default factor 1.3 and repeats until a gap-one pass makes no swaps, matching the comb_sort variant.

The C source prints counts for nonnegative values; C++ finds the minimum and maximum and returns a separate array; Rust sorts unsigned keys in place with a caller-provided maximum. The local workload and contract use signed 64-bit keys in [-128, 128] and a shared histogram scratch area.

The checked C source counts writes, C++ returns a sorted vector copy, and Rust mutates a slice. All use rank counting and cycle placement; local ports use a shared in-place signed 64-bit contract with bounds-checked duplicate skips.

The pinned C-Sharp class counts smaller values and rotates items to their sorted positions, matching cycle_sort. Its duplicate-skip loop lacks an array-bound check and can advance past the end; the shared benchmark contract handles duplicate skips safely.

The Dart and Python sources perform the same decimal-to-radix conversion as decimal_to_any_base for the normalized base-2-through-36 contract. This candidate aliases decimal_to_any_base to avoid duplicating the same algorithm.

The C and Java sources convert decimal values to a requested radix. The shared contract supports nonnegative signed 64-bit values and radices 2-36, emitting uppercase prefix-free digits; local ports use portable integer division and remainder.

The pinned Java source uses a LIFO character stack after successive division. The shared contract preserves radix 2 through 16 and upper-case output, while widening the number input to nonnegative signed 64-bit for a common cross-language ABI.

Inspected the pinned C, both C++ repository copies, Dart, Java, JavaScript, PHP, Python, Ruby, Rust, and Swift sources. They produce a binary digit string or decimal-encoded bit digits; some print or return an empty value for zero, and negative-input behavior varies. The shared contract writes an unprefixed most-significant-first ASCII representation for nonnegative signed 64-bit inputs, spells zero as "0", rejects negatives with -1, and returns -2 when the caller output buffer is too small.

The pinned sources convert by repeated division and remainder. The C++ console example uses uppercase digits and interactive I/O; the Python source uses lowercase with a 0x prefix and supports negative values. The local contract writes prefix-free lowercase hexadecimal digits for nonnegative signed 64-bit inputs into a caller buffer, returns -1 for negatives, and -2 for insufficient capacity.

The pinned sources repeatedly divide decimal input by eight and emit octal digits; the Python source adds a 0o prefix and constructs place values through floating point, while the C console example fails to print zero. The local contract writes prefix-free octal digits for nonnegative signed 64-bit inputs into a caller buffer, returns -1 for negatives, and -2 for insufficient capacity.

The pinned C++ implementation traverses an undirected adjacency list recursively from a fixed start; the Rust source named depth_first_search uses a deque as a stack and returns history through a requested target. The shared contract normalizes both APIs to a complete directed recursive-preorder traversal with ascending neighbors.

The inspected C source uses an adjacency matrix, signed int distances, and a static remembered minimum-vertex index; C++ uses a priority queue for a source-to-target query but stores queue distances as int while its distance vector is int64_t; Rust returns a predecessor map for reachable vertices using an ordered set. The local contract standardizes all-source distances, nonnegative signed 64-bit weights, and explicit overflow and invalid-input statuses. Nine ports use the same flat-edge-list, no-allocation minimum-selection variant.

Reviewed all seven pinned disjoint_set sources in C++ (two repositories), C-Sharp, Julia, PHP, Python, and TypeScript. They implement the same partition and set-union behavior as union_find, with path compression plus rank or size heuristics in most versions; C++ uses a one-based universe, while object-based versions carry values in nodes. This candidate aliases the shared zero-based union_find contract.

Reviewed the pinned Java and Rust disjoint_set_union sources. Both implement the same partition and merge behavior as union_find, using node objects and rank in Java and indexed nodes with union by size in Rust. This candidate aliases the shared zero-based union_find contract.

Inspected the pinned C++ sources in both C++ repositories, the C-Sharp BigInteger implementation, and the Python recursive and iterative forms. They compute the same-parity product with 0!! = 1; arbitrary-precision inputs and exception behavior vary. The shared scalar contract accepts 0 through 33, returns the exact signed 64-bit value, and returns -1 for negative inputs or values above 33.

The 14 pinned implementations share a doubly linked list structure, while their APIs vary across positional insertion/deletion, end operations, search, reversal, and size. The benchmark normalizes this family to append/prepend, pop at either end, remove the first matching value, contains, and length; its bounded index-based node pool is a portable benchmark representation.
The pinned PHP source intends the same Sieve of Eratosthenes, but leaves 1 in its returned array. The shared contract uses corrected sieve semantics and counts primes from 2.

The inspected sources implement exponential range expansion followed by a search in the bounded region, with varying element widths, APIs, and search details. The local benchmark standardizes ascending signed 64-bit input and returns any matching index, or -1 when absent.

The inspected C source prints arbitrary-precision decimal digits, and C++ uses recursion with an input limit of 20. The local scalar contract uses an iterative signed 64-bit product for inputs 0 through 20 and returns -1 outside that range.

Reviewed all seven pinned Fenwick-tree sources in C++ (two repositories), Java, JavaScript, Julia, Python, and Rust. They share point-add updates and prefix or range sums but differ in public indexing and whether ranges are inclusive or half-open. The shared contract standardizes zero-based point additions and inclusive range sums, with a bounded signed-64-bit workload.

The inspected C source uses a one-based argument and naive recursion; C++ uses zero-based naive recursion, and the Rust source includes multiple indexing conventions and variants. The local scalar contract defines the classical zero-based sequence, uses the iterative recurrence, and returns -1 outside 0 through 92.

The pinned C source computes the zero-based Fibonacci sequence by recursive fast doubling. The C++ copies with the same filename instead use a stateful linear recurrence and treat indices 0 through 2 identically. The benchmark selects the C source’s exact zero-based fast-doubling behavior with an input bound of 0 through 92 and ports that method to all target languages using fixed-width 64-bit intermediates.

The checked C, C++, and Rust implementations use Fibonacci-number probes over sorted arrays, with differing index widths and result APIs. The local contract standardizes ascending signed 64-bit input, an index or -1 result, and explicit empty-input handling.

The pinned implementations scan arrays for their maximum; the Python source provides iterative and recursive versions and raises an error for an empty list. The local contract uses an iterative scan over 1..512 signed 64-bit values, returning -1 for an empty or oversized array.

The pinned implementations scan arrays for their minimum; the Python source provides iterative and recursive versions, while the Dart entry prints the result and assumes a nonempty list. The local contract uses an iterative scan over 1..512 signed 64-bit values, returning -1 for an empty or oversized array.

The pinned C, C++, and Rust sources implement the Floyd-Warshall recurrence with matrix or map graphs. The benchmark normalizes them to a bounded directed edge-list contract, chooses the minimum parallel edge, and returns one source row after all-pairs computation in all nine target languages.

The seven pinned implementations solve fractional knapsack by ordering items by value-to-weight ratio and taking a fraction of the final item when needed. The two C++ files were discovered under the generic knapsack filename and are cross-listed here because they implement the fractional problem. The second Python filename is another implementation of the same greedy algorithm. The benchmark standardizes positive integer weights, nonnegative integer values, exact ratio comparisons, and a six-decimal fixed-point result.

This second Python source uses the fractional knapsack greedy strategy: it orders by value-to-weight ratio, takes whole items while they fit, and takes a fraction of the next item. Its fractional selection semantics match the shared fractional_knapsack contract on the benchmark’s bounded positive-weight integer input domain.

The pinned C source uses recursive Euclid with signed int inputs and returns the first input when the second is zero. The Zig source uses iterative Euclid with unsigned inputs, supports one zero input, and asserts that both are not zero. The local contract uses iterative Euclid over nonnegative values through INT64_MAX, defines gcd(0, 0) as zero, and returns a signed 64-bit result. All nine ports use the shared binary-scalar ABI.

The pinned C++ source folds pairwise Euclidean GCD, and the Rust source recursively folds the same operation. The Python source instead intersects prime-factor counts. The shared benchmark uses a nonempty array of positive signed 32-bit values, which avoids the source variants’ different zero, negative, and empty-input conventions, and standardizes the pairwise Euclidean fold.

The checked C and C++ sources walk adjacent pairs, moving forward when ordered and swapping backward when not. The local contract guards the beginning of the sequence and sorts signed 64-bit values in place.
The pinned C-Sharp class advances across ordered adjacent values and swaps backward over inversions, matching the gnome_sort contract.

The pinned C source implements Hamming distance for null-terminated strings, while the C++ and Rust bit-manipulation sources implement both string and unsigned 64-bit integer variants. The local benchmark selects the unsigned integer variant, counts all 64 bit positions, and uses two unsigned 64-bit ABI inputs. The C port supplies that integer contract separately from the upstream C string routine.

The checked C source uses a one-based heap in an interactive example, while C++ builds and extracts from a zero-based max heap. The local benchmark standardizes in-place ascending sorting of signed 64-bit values with a zero-based heap.

The pinned C source constructs a max heap by repeatedly inserting each value with sift-up, then extracts maxima with sift-down. This construction strategy is distinct from the existing bottom-up heap_sort benchmark. The source uses int8_t values and an 8-bit length in a random demo; the shared benchmark uses signed 64-bit values in place and caps length at 1024.

The pinned C-Sharp class builds a max heap bottom-up, repeatedly moves the maximum to the end, and restores the heap. It shares the canonical heap_sort contract; its generic comparer supplies the numeric ordering.

Inspected the pinned Dart source. It maps hexadecimal characters to binary groups and accepts a leading sign. The cataloged Rust source path does not resolve at its pinned revision, so it was not used to infer the shared contract. The benchmark accepts a most-significant-first hexadecimal digit array of length 1 through 16, rejects values above INT64_MAX, and writes canonical prefix-free binary output.

Inspected the pinned Dart, PHP, and Python sources. They convert hexadecimal digit strings to decimal values, with differing whitespace and signed-input handling. The cataloged Rust source URL does not resolve at its pinned revision, so it was not used to infer the shared contract. The benchmark uses a most-significant-first numeric digit array, accepts digits 0 through 15 and nonnegative values through INT64_MAX, and returns -1 for malformed, empty, overlength, or overflowing inputs.

Inspected the pinned C and Dart sources. The C console program converts through a binary-looking numeric intermediate; Dart converts through decimal using floating-point powers and accepts a leading sign. The cataloged Rust source path does not resolve at its pinned revision, so it was not used to infer the shared contract. The benchmark accepts a most-significant-first hexadecimal digit array of length 1 through 16, rejects values above INT64_MAX, and writes prefix-free octal output.

The checked C and C++ sources build a sorted prefix by shifting larger values and inserting the next key. The local contract sorts signed 64-bit values in ascending order in place and preserves equal-key order.

The pinned C source recursively sorts each prefix and inserts its last value. The C++ source with the same filename is iterative insertion sort, so this benchmark adopts the recursive C method and ports that contract across all nine languages. Sorting is stable, ascending, in place over signed 64-bit values, with workload lengths capped at 256 to bound recursive stack depth.
The pinned C-Sharp class uses adjacent exchanges to insert each value into the sorted prefix. It shares the canonical stable insertion_sort ordering contract.

The pinned JavaScript source repeatedly divides the absolute value by a numeric base and concatenates decimal remainders; for nonnegative inputs in bases 2 through 10, it emits the same canonical digits as decimal_to_any_base. Its negative handling is outside the shared nonnegative contract.
The pinned Python source performs the same repeated division by -2 and negative-remainder correction as base_neg2_conversion. It shares the canonical negabinary conversion contract.

The inspected implementations interpolate a probe position over sorted integer values but use differing widths and result APIs. The local benchmark standardizes strictly ascending signed 64-bit values, explicit empty handling, and an arithmetic-bound precondition satisfied by the declared workload.

Inspected the pinned Java, JavaScript, Python, and TypeScript sources. They test parity using a bit check or modulo and return a boolean; Python and TypeScript additionally validate integer inputs. The shared benchmark uses the signed 64-bit integer domain and returns 1 for even and 0 for odd, covering the full range without taking absolute values.

Inspected the pinned JavaScript, Python, and Rust sources. Each tests whether the input has exactly one set bit; their zero behavior differs from the shared positive-power contract. This filename is consolidated with power_of_two under the same explicit n > 0 predicate.

The pinned Kotlin and Lua sources named is_prime test the same mathematical primality predicate. They share prime_check’s explicit signed 32-bit positive input range and result contract, including negative inputs returning false.

The pinned Python iter_merge_sort grows adjacent runs in iterative bottom-up passes and merges them pairwise, matching the strategy represented by merge_sort_nr. Its list slicing and repeated pop(0) add copying overhead; the benchmark uses a fixed scratch buffer and a signed 64-bit in-place contract.

The checked sources use square-root-sized blocks followed by a linear scan, but their index types and empty-input handling differ. The local contract standardizes ascending signed 64-bit input, any matching index or -1, and empty-input behavior.

candidates.review_notes: The ten-repository filename group mixes knapsack variants. Its Go, Java, Python, Ruby, Rust, Solidity, TypeScript, and Zig sources implement 0/1 knapsack; the two C++ files implement fractional knapsack and are cross-listed with that candidate. Python recursive knapsack defaults to 0/1 and also offers an optional unbounded mode. This candidate aliases the shared 0/1 tabulation contract; fractional_knapsack has a separate benchmark.

Inspected the pinned Java tabulation source. Its two-dimensional table uses the standard 0/1 recurrence over items and capacities. The pinned C++ 0_1_knapsack and Kotlin zero_one_knapsack_problem sources use the same bottom-up recurrence; their source filenames are recorded as aliases. The shared implementation stores one row and scans capacities downward so each item is still used at most once. The mixed generic knapsack filename candidate is also an alias for its 0/1 variants; its two C++ fractional-knapsack files are tracked under fractional_knapsack.

The inspected TheAlgorithms implementations calculate the least common multiple for integer inputs, but their multiply-before-divide formulations can overflow fixed-width integer types. The shared benchmark defines nonnegative signed-64-bit inputs, returns zero when either input is zero, computes after reducing by the gcd, and returns -1 when the mathematical result exceeds INT64_MAX. Portable implementations are present in all nine local languages.

The Rust reference recursively folds a nonempty slice and computes a * b / gcd(a, b) using usize, so empty input is unsupported and intermediate multiplication can overflow. The shared contract defines the empty identity, zero behavior, nonnegative signed-64-bit inputs, and an explicit overflow result; the nine local ports reduce by the GCD before checked multiplication.

The two C++ references compute sum(LCM(i, n)) for 1 <= i <= n using the weighted Euler-totient identity and accept a uint16_t input. Their sieve and accumulation allocate arrays. The shared contract returns -1 outside 1..65535; the local ports use the same identity, enumerate divisor pairs, and calculate the needed totients by factorization without host-specific instructions or dynamic allocation.
The pinned C, Julia, Kotlin, and TypeScript sources use the longest common subsequence recurrence. They share the canonical benchmark contract, which measures the length of an LCS.

The Java reference provides recursive and iterative implementations of L(0)=L(1)=1 and L(n)=L(n-1)+L(n-2)+1, and returns int. The shared contract extends exact values to index 89 with signed 64-bit results and returns -1 outside 0..89; local ports use the iterative recurrence.

The C source offers both start + t * (end - start) and an alternate weighted-sum expression; Go uses the weighted-sum expression with float64. The shared contract selects the classic expression over bounded finite binary64 inputs, and defines an input-scaled tolerance so rounding remains comparable near cancellation.

The JavaScript source recursively constructs the Cartesian product of keypad letters for digits 2 through 9. It is the same algorithm as the Java phone-number candidate and shares that benchmark contract; this filename is retained as an alias to avoid duplicating one algorithm in the benchmark catalog.

The Java source recursively enumerates phone keypad letters as a Cartesian product, matching the JavaScript letter_combination candidate. The shared contract uses digits 2 through 9, ordered fixed-width byte output, zero combinations for empty input, and rejects invalid digits.

The Java source's traverse method uses a FIFO queue, captures the queue size before each depth, processes children left-to-right, and returns one value list per level. The same file also contains a recursive printGivenLevel helper; this benchmark selects the queue-based grouped traversal and records flat values with level offsets.

The Lua and R filename match uses the same unit-cost insertion/deletion/substitution distance as the canonical candidate. The shared ASCII contract removes differences in character indexing. This source filename is retained as an alias to share one benchmark contract.

Inspected the pinned C-Sharp, F-Sharp, Java, both JavaScript, Nim, Python, Rust, Lua, R, and Go source files. The standard implementations compute the minimum insertion, deletion, and substitution cost; Java also exposes an optimized implementation, and Go accepts configurable costs that reduce to ordinary Levenshtein distance when all three costs are one. The shared benchmark restricts inputs to ASCII bytes so byte-indexed and character-indexed sources use identical units. Adjacent transposition support is cataloged separately as Damerau-Levenshtein distance.

The Go source exposes insertion, substitution, and deletion weights; setting each weight to one gives the same ordinary Levenshtein distance as the canonical candidate. This source filename is retained as an alias to share one benchmark contract.
The checked source implementations scan in order and return the first matching position. The local benchmark standardizes a signed 64-bit index result, with -1 for no match.

The pinned JavaScript and Scala sources implement the linear (Euler) sieve and return primes through an inclusive limit. Rust also stores the minimum-prime-factor table for later factorization. Its inner loop stops at p > i rather than p > minimum_prime_factor[i], so the local ports use the standard bound that marks each composite once. The shared contract returns the prime count for limits 0..4096; limits below two normalize to zero.

candidates.review_notes: The pinned Python source evaluates base -2 binary digits as signed positional values. The cross-language contract accepts a most-significant-first bit array of up to 63 digits, ensuring every possible prefix and final value fits signed 64-bit.
